title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
talk_summary: MiniMax's engineer argues model speed must be judged by end-to-end job time and quality, using a fixed research-report task with source and calculation checks. The transferable method is to benchmark usable outputs, include retries and human fixes, and inspect latency tails and critical quality slices rather than model-only speed.

takeaways.what_they_do: They fix the source reports, information cutoff, and acceptance criteria before comparing models, then measure whether the finished report is usable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fix this question on the source reports and use the same information cutoff and agree on what makes a report acceptable

takeaways.what_they_do: They include retrieval, tool calls, retries, failed attempts, and human repair time in the cost of producing an acceptable report.
takeaways.evidence_quote: include all the failed attempts in the cost of producing uh of producing this acceptable reports

takeaways.what_they_do: They test concurrency and show aggregate output throughput can rise while tail first-token latency worsens sharply.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the P95 weight for the first token rises. It goes from about 1.5 seconds to 11.3 seconds
takeaways.numbers: Concurrency 32 to 64: total output/sec +1.9x; P95 first-token wait 1.5s to 11.3s (~8x).

takeaways.what_they_do: They inspect specific score drops hidden by near-identical averages, such as a sign-score regression.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the average scores actually is almost the same but the sign score there it drops like 6.6 percentage
takeaways.numbers: Sign score drops ~6.6 percentage points while average is almost unchanged.

takeaways.what_they_do: They move an important passage to different positions in a long input and ask the same question again to verify retrieval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: move this important passage to different places in the input and then ask the same question again
takeaways.numbers: 39 requests passed; longest inputs about 830k tokens.

takeaways.what_they_do: They compare reasoning-effort settings on the same tasks and record the accuracy/token tradeoff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: high uses fewer up output tokens than the max but the accuracy actually fell from 80% to 68%
takeaways.numbers: High reasoning vs max: fewer output tokens, accuracy 80% to 68%.
